## Criteria

**AC-1: UNMET (one BLOCKING gap).** `docs/setup-from-zero.md` is a single ordered checklist with 12 steps. It links the existing pages, and README.md and docs/README.md list it first. **HUMAN** steps say exactly what the human must do. judgement.reason: Verified in the checkout: src/main-guard.ts gives a revert one attempt — abandon() fires at the approveRevert catch ("the revert approver could not approve revert PR #N") and the mergeRevert catch ("GitHub refused to merge revert PR #N"), closes the revert PR, records `abandoned`, and is never retried; mainGuardAttention + src/daemon/cycle-delivery.ts:81-86 raise exactly one unowned line per abandonment. Git corroborates the outcome: merge #794 (GY-1306) landed 2026-10-05T18:27:45Z and main's next first-parent merge is #795 at 20:16:50Z (109 min, the longest gap in that stretch); "Merge pull request #796" is absent from main's history and no revert commit of 45284c9a68 exists on main, so the revert PR opened 18:31:14Z never landed and an unrelated merge recovered main. GY-1317's revert did land later (ec67aa824a, 21:18:35Z), so the failure is conditional — a single transient refusal on the approval/merge call converts to a full abandonment. Not fixed by GY-1291 (delivered 11:38Z; added the independent approver under last-push protection, which the 18:27Z window postdates), not covered by open GY-1331 (soak approvals) or delivered GY-1328/1329 (rerun 403s). All three proposed changes are scoped code work in src/main-guard.ts, src/github.ts and cycle-delivery.ts with no operator action. P1: with the queue removed (GY-1235) the guard is the only automated recovery for red main, and one refusal left production main's required check red ~109 min, recurring twice on 2026-10-05.

reviews.body:
Independent review of GY-1332 at 17374fbd8c15.

**AC-1: met.** In `src/main-guard.ts`, an approval refused by the approver App still tries `mergeRevert`, which is the App's ruleset-bypass merge path. When the merge is refused, the guard appends the refusal to `refusals`, drops the cached `pr@head` approval and leaves the revert `opened`. On the next tick it re-verifies the inverse, approves again and merges again. The revert is abandoned as `approval-refused` only after `revertLandingAttempts` (3) refusals. Failing checks, conflicts, timeouts and a non-inverse diff still abandon on the first look. `unit:main-guard-approval-refusal-retry` covers each of these cases.

**AC-2: unmet (BLOCKING, reliability).** `src/daemon/cycle-delivery.ts:84-86` still passes every abandoned revert through `mainGuardAttention(abandoned, since)`. `since` is the `at` of the oldest retained resolved row once the cursor holds `retainedActions` (500) resolved rows. On a long-running loop that is the steady state, because `pruneDaemonState` keeps it at 500. The filter in `src/main-guard.ts` (`!(Date.parse(revert.settledAt ?? revert.at) <= since)`) compares the revert's **settledAt**, not its row's `at`. A red revert's own row is re-recorded every cycle and is never pruned. But once 500 other resolved rows newer than the abandonment have built up, `since` passes `settledAt`. The revert then drops out of `mainGuardAttention` entirely, and the line stops being raised while main is still red. This is the failure GY-1332 was filed for: the line goes quiet while main stays red. AC-2 requires the line "on every cycle until the failing check on main passes again". The new doc comment ("a red line is re-recorded every cycle, so its row is never the oldest") is about row pruning, not this filter. The soak does not catch it, because it adds its `retainedActions + 20` filler rows only after the line has recovered. Follow-up finding: src/quarantine.ts:311 — loopEndedAttempt counts any non-lapsed worker exhaustion for the epoch as the loop's ending, including one a worker records itself through `blocked`, so the docstring's "only a coordinator or an admin records" overstates it; the verified-gone pairing still bounds the risk.
Follow-up finding: src/daemon/cycle-reclaim.ts:140 — settleEndedAttemptFence polls inline for up to endedFenceWaitMs (10s) per ended attempt, so a cycle that ends several fenced attempts can stall for N×10s; a shared per-cycle bound would cap it.

Independent Graphyard review of GY-1155 at ae7109a30e1e (base 38f3e6d2c6be, policy rev 4).

The PR's own change at this head is the same as at 51c8013, except that two soak plan keys (`breaksMain`, `infrastructure`) are dropped. Main removed those keys with the optimistic-merge revert. I re-read the full source diff against the merge base 6cf7da0dd2.

## Criteria

**AC-1: met.** The loop ends attempts in four places, and each one calls `settleEndedAttemptFence` (src/daemon/cycle-reclaim.ts:132) in the same action:
- `endWorkerAttempt`, for idle-with-lease and credential-blocked endings
- the quota failover in `closeStep`
- the orphaned-supervisor stop
- `closeExitedWorkerSessions`, for a submitted attempt

The function judges `endedRecord(...)`: the ended lease is dropped, and the loop's preserve exhaustion and closed handle are added. It polls within a 10s bound until the host verifies the supervisor gone, then posts autosettle. It then nulls `item.containmentQuarantine`, so the faults pass in the same cycle records nothing for that epoch. If the settle misses, the reclaim step's `settling` predicate retries the item without waiting out the grace window.

**AC-2: met.** `containmentSettlementRefusals` (src/quarantine.ts:355) waives the grace and launch-window refusals only when `loopEndedAttempt` and `supervisorVerifiedGone` both hold. `loopEndedAttempt` excludes `leaseLapsedEnding`, and its closed handle must

findings.text: src/quarantine.ts:299 — loopEndedAttempt treats any non-lapsed worker exhaustion as the loop's ending, including the one a worker's own `blocked` command records (recordedBy the worker), so the docstring's "only a coordinator or an admin records" is false; check `recordedBy`/`owner` against the worker if the waiver should stay strictly on the loop's record.

src/daemon/cycle-reclaim.ts:134 — the in-action probe loop polls synchronously for up to endedFenceWaitMs (10s) per ended attempt, so a cycle ending several fenced attempts can stall for N×10s; consider one shared bound per cycle or deferring to the reclaim step after the first probe.

src/quarantine.ts:311 — loopEndedAttempt counts any non-lapsed worker exhaustion for the epoch as the loop's ending, including one a worker records through its own `blocked` command, so the docstring's "only a coordinator or an admin records" overstates it; checking `recordedBy` would keep the waiver strictly on the loop's record (the verified-gone pairing still bounds the risk).

src/daemon/cycle-reclaim.ts:140 — settleEndedAttemptFence polls inline for up to endedFenceWaitMs (10s) per ended attempt, so a cycle that ends several fenced attempts can stall for N×10s; a shared per-cycle bound, or deferring to the reclaim step after the first probe, would cap it.

src/quarantine.ts:299 — `loopEndedAttempt` counts any role-'worker' exhaustion for the epoch, but the engine's worker-issued `blocked` command (engine.ts `if (command === 'blocked')`) also writes one, with recordedBy set to the worker. The docstring's "only a coordinator or an admin records" is therefore inaccurate. The waiver still needs the lease ended on the record and the supervisor verified gone, and the credential-blocked ending relies on that worker record, which is why this is not blocking. A tighter rule would accept a worker-recorded exhaustion only together with the loop's `closed as failed:` handle, or a coordinator's recordedBy.

src/quarantine.ts:300 — the "closed by the loop:" / "closed as failed:" handle test matches outcome text only. The session owner may rewrite its own handle while it holds the lease, so the text is not proof that the loop wrote it. Bind it to the recorder, as the observation fields are, rather than to a string prefix.

src/daemon/cycle-reclaim.ts:134 — `settleEndedAttemptFence` blocks the loop cycle for up to `endedFenceWaitMs` (10s) per ended attempt whose supervisor does not exit promptly. Several such endings in one cycle add up serially, and the bound is wall-clock (`Date.now`), not the cycle's clock. Consider one shared bound per cycle, or deferring to the reclaim step after the first probe.

src/quarantine.ts:299 — loopEndedAttempt counts any role-'worker' exhaustion for the epoch, but the engine's worker-issued `blocked` command also writes one, with recordedBy set to the worker. The docstring's claim that only a coordinator or an admin records one is therefore inaccurate. Accepting a worker-recorded exhaustion only together with the loop's close handle, or with a coordinator's recordedBy, would keep the waiver strictly on the loop's record.

src/quarantine.ts:300 — the "closed by the loop:" / "closed as failed:" handle test matches outcome text only, which a lease-holding session owner can rewrite. Bind it to the recorder rather than to a string prefix.

src/daemon/cycle-reclaim.ts:134 — settleEndedAttemptFence blocks the cycle for up to endedFenceWaitMs (10s, wall-clock) per ended attempt whose supervisor does not exit promptly, and several such endings add up serially. A shared per-cycle bound, or deferring to the reclaim step after the first probe, would cap that.

src/quarantine.ts:300 — the closed-session leg of `loopEndedAttempt` trusts the handle's outcome text, but `recordSession` lets the handle's own principal (the worker) write state and outcome. A worker could write "closed by the loop: …" itself. It gains nothing while the supervisor-verified-gone and lease checks stand, but the "loop's own record" should be checked by provenance (who wrote the handle), not by prefix.

src/daemon/cycle-reclaim.ts:134 — `settleEndedAttemptFence` polls the host for up to 10 s inside the cycle whenever the stopped supervisor is not yet verified gone. Several endings in one cycle stall it by up to 10 s each. Consider bounding the total wait per cycle and leaving the rest to the reclaim step.

src/daemon/cycle-sessions.ts:257 — the orphaned-supervisor path settles in-action only when `preserveInterruptedAttempt` returns a done action. When the epoch was already preserved (it returns null), the same-action settle is skipped and only the reclaim step settles it, on a later cycle.

reviews.body:
**BLOCKING: closeStep's sighting marker turns into a permanent `action:close` fault and restarts its own timer (src/daemon/cycle-sessions.ts:52-62; affects AC-2 and the per-cycle soak rule)**
Follow-up finding: src/master-resources.ts:125 — `unownedPaneConfirmMs` duplicates `launchAppearanceMs` as a literal 120_000, and only a test asserts they are equal. Importing it, or deriving one from the other, would keep them in step.

REQUEST_CHANGES on aaa4cb14cb24 for GY-1166. One BLOCKING reliability defect, in the per-cycle closeStep path, that also affects AC-2.

The first sighting is stored with `record(state, seenKey, { kind: 'close', state: 'started', … })`. On every cycle, `runCycle` calls `reconcilePendingActions(state, snapshot.work, clock)` (src/daemon/cycle.ts:120) before `closeStep` (cycle.ts:195). That function treats any `started` entry that isn't a launcher key as an interrupted action. It has no branch for `close`, so it falls to the `else` branch and rewrites the row as `state: 'indeterminate'` with `at` set to that cycle's clock (src/daemon/reconcile.ts:78-81). That causes three problems:
1. `storeAction` → `noteActionOutcome` opens an `action:close` fault instance for every sighted pane and records it in `faults.failing` (src/model/fault-record.ts:53-61).
2. `pruneDaemonState` removes only `done` and `failed` rows, so an `indeterminate` row stays forever. Once the pane is closed it never reports a recognised status again, so the new `delete state.actions[seenKey]` never runs, and the row and its failing run stay for good. That is one leaked cursor row and one standing fault for every pane reclaimed this way. This item exists to stop recurring faults on exactly these panes.
3. Because `at` is reset to the reconcile cycle, the `launchAppearanceMs` wait really starts one cycle late. At the observed 7–11 min cadence, closeStep closes the pane at the earliest two cycles after the first sighting, past `nameReclaimBoundMs`. That misses AC-2's "within nameReclai

findings.text: src/daemon/cycle-sessions.ts:45 — `exited:${profile}:${pane}` sighting rows stay in state `started` after their pane is closed, and `pruneDaemonState` only retires done/failed rows. Each closed unrecognised-status pane therefore leaves one action row for good. This pre-dates the change for agentless panes, but the change widens it to every unknown/no-status holder, so the rows should be dropped once the pane is closed or gone.

src/daemon/cycle-sessions.ts:52 — unlike reclaim step 4, closeStep has no `launchingWorker`-style guard. A worker whose runtime is present but which Herdr reports `unknown`, and which has not claimed its lease within 120 s of its pane first being seen, would be closed as a leak. AC-4 is met by the launchAppearanceMs wait, but a slow claim on a runtime Herdr cannot classify is not covered.

tests/soak.test.ts:270 — the soak Herdr model only produces `unknown` with no runtime and `idle`. The new holder shapes (`unknown` with a runtime present, and no status) are never exercised over a simulated day.

src/master-resources.ts:131 — when Herdr is unreadable (`observed.agents` null), the `evidence` set is empty and retention reaps held names' records. The reaped-record path recovers this, but keeping retention back for one pass while Herdr is blind would keep the close reason precise.

src/daemon/cycle-sessions.ts:45 — an `exited:` sighting row whose pane was closed (or disappeared) while still unrecognised is never deleted. It persists as a `started` row and is never pruned by `pruneDaemonState` (only done/failed rows are). The widening produces more of these rows than the old agentless-only shape did, so they should be cleared when the pane closes.

src/master-resources.ts:668 — the retention exception keeps the newest record on any name a pane holds, including a `working` pane that is never closed. A long-lived runaway holder therefore pins its record indefinitely. This is bounded by the number of panes, but it should be stated in the agent-names resource reading.

src/daemon/cycle-sessions.ts:45 — the `exited:${profile}:${pane}` sighting row stays in state `started` after its pane is closed. The pane then disappears, so the `!unrecognized` delete never runs, and `pruneDaemonState` only retires `done`/`failed` rows. With this change every unknown/no-status pane, not just exited runtimes, leaves one such row, so state.actions grows by one row per closed pane over a long run. Delete the sighting when the close succeeds, or sweep sightings whose pane Herdr no longer lists.

Follow-up finding: src/main-guard.ts:374 — when the revert of B has merged but main is still red because of a later merge C, `readMain` still names B, which is already reverted, so C waits until main is green again.
Follow-up finding: src/github.ts:2526 — `mergeRevert` labels the `Graphyard / merge` verdict "optimistic-merge revert" even for GY-1250 reverts, which is cosmetic.
Follow-up finding: src/main-guard.ts:270 — `reopenReverted` does not set `work.reopened` the way the GY-500 path does, so the rework reason is only stored on `mainGuardReverts`.

Review of GY-1250 at 3515ada78fa66d195a74e15f8acecfe9c0df55a3.

**AC-1: met.** `src/main-guard.ts` and `tests/main-guard.test.ts` are new. `readMain` names the first-parent merge that fails a required check while its parent passed. `openMainRevert` builds that merge's inverse (the first parent's tree on top of the merge) and merges it onto main's tip on a `graphyard-revert/` branch, so later merges stay. `mergeRevert` merges it as the App only after `commitVerdict` on the revert head passes. `reopenReverted` withdraws the delivery and returns the item to `ready`, and `mainGuardReason` names the failing check and the merge commit. The `unit:main-guard-reverts-breaking-merge` test runs A→B→C against a fake GitHub where B breaks `test`, and asserts that B is reverted, not A or C, and that B's item is reopened. CI does not cancel pushes to main (ci.yml concurrency), so a cancelled run cannot be mistaken for a failing merge.

**AC-2: not met. BLOCKING (AC-2, and the soak rule for per-cycle behaviour).** A revert is closed after its one attempt in every case: conflict, failed checks, an hour without a result, or a refused merge. The guard also handles the nex

risks: GY-1233 removes the optimistic merge lane and its main guard concurrently: src/optimistic-merge.ts (postMergeVerdict, failedConclusions, reopenReverted, the `reopened` Work field declaration) and src/github.ts guardMain may be deleted or rewritten while this item builds — re-check at build time, copy what vanished, and expect conflicts around the shared processJob hook and imports

docs page budgets: docs/delivery.md is 1113/1200 words and docs/github.md is exactly 1200/1200 — AC-3's text must fit inside delivery.md's ~87-word headroom (or trim within the same page); tests/docs-budget.test.ts fails a page over budget, which is the very failure this item exists to stop repeating

The bypass must stay minimal and audited: publishing `Graphyard / merge`/graphyard/landable success before the revert PR's own required checks pass would let the App merge anything; publish the verdict only after the revert's own checks pass, and record every step (opened, pending, merged, closed) as its own ledger event

The revert PR's own CI may never go green: a second culprit in the window, required checks that need an up-to-date branch, or flaky checks — one attempt, then close the PR and raise the one attention line; never retry the same red window

Squash vs merge commits: under GitHub delivery autoMergeMethod() defaults to MERGE but GITHUB_MERGE_METHOD may set SQUASH — the culprit can be a two-parent merge commit (revert with first parent) or a single-parent squash commit; the old guard refused REBASE bases outright, keep that refusal

Culprit identification by mergedAt can disagree with first-parent ancestry when merges land out of order or the observation clock is skewed (delivery carries repositoryClockOffsetMs) — order the window by the merge commits' ancestry on the base branch, or by mergedAt with the recorded offset applied; a wrong culprit reverts an innocent merge

Reopen must be idempotent and must not fight the existing hand-revert reading (observation.revertedDelivery / merged-reverted attention for a non-done merged item): only the guard's own merged revert reopens; reopening twice, or reopening an item whose content is already restored, corrupts the record

Cost: commitChecks per merge commit per tick; cache verdicts, re-read only pending commits, write state rows only on change (soak asserts bounded reads/writes: at most a few commits' checks per cycle, one row per change)
Exactly one attention line per abandoned revert: the action/ledger key must include the culprit merge sha so the next red main re-arms; a key without it deduplicates every later incident into silence

Multiple server replicas could run the guard concurrently; keep idempotency through head-bound merges, PR reuse, verdict-identity checks and value-identity ledger rows (guardMain's approach) instead of adding a lease

The reopened item must re-enter the pipeline cleanly: withdraw delivery, record the rework round, clear submission/candidate/observation/authorization fields as reopenReverted does, keep history, and leave the merged PR closed (it cannot take commits) so the next round opens a fresh PR from the current base
cycle-delivery.ts is 453 of its 800 budgeted lines; the guard-aware hold and attention must be tight, and any shared helper belongs in src/main-guard.ts

The new test file must be Postgres-free if it fakes the engine (the optimistic-merge harness pattern) or it inherits the embedded-Postgres cost and shutdown-order rules; either way its timing-baseline line must be recorded or ci-shards fails at ≥90% coverage
Do not run the guard for non-GitHub deliveries: without the marker gate the guarded merge/queue already keeps main green; running both guards would double-revert

A hand fix landing while the guard's revert is in flight (race): the revert merge is head-bound and refused if its head moved, and the guard must re-read the window before opening a revert so it never reverts a merge whose breakage a later commit already repaired
brief.approach: Build the guard as the GitHub-delivery sibling of GY-500, in the exact shapes this checkout already proves. (1) src/main-guard.ts, new module opening `// Concern: keeping main green under GitHub delivery — the post-merge main guard`. It holds: the pure state machine (window of merges since the last green commit, `green|pending|culprit|reverting|merged|abandoned`; the first failing merge since the last green is the culprit — direct reading of each merge commit's checks, no bisection needed since every main commit gets its own push-run); a copied/adapted `postMergeVerdict`+`failedConclusions` (copy them in; GY-1233 deletes their home); a `declare module './model/work.js'` ambient `Work.mainGuard`/`reopened` extension (re-declare `reopened` here if GY-1233 removed it, with source like 'main-guard-revert'); and the runner `guardDeliveryMain(engine, github, now)` modeled line-for-line on `guardMain`: narrow engine interface (`store.list`, `pool.query` for its own `main-guard.*` ledger kinds with the value-identity dedup, and a `reopenDelivered(id, reopen)` transaction that withdraws delivery, calls `recordRework`, sets stage back to ready, clears submission/candidate/observation/mergeAuthorization/mergeExecution/queue fields exactly as `reopenReverted` does, writes `reopened={reason naming the failing check, the merge commit and the revert PR, at, source}`, re-evaluates and records the dispatch). On abandonment (revert conflicts or its checks fail) it records one `main-guard.abandoned` ledger row and the marker on the kept delivery, then releases: the guard's key is the last green sha, so the next red main is handled afresh. (2) src/github.ts: add `openMergeRevert(culprit, reason)` — generalize `openRevert` to take the files from the culprit commit's own diff (`/commits/{sha}` files; first-parent tree restore handles merge commits, single-parent handles squash; keep the REBASE-method refusal), same `graphyard-revert/` branch and idempotent PR reuse; add `closePullRequest(pr, reason)`; reuse `mergeRevert`'s head-bound sequence but publish the `Graphyard / merge` verdict and `upsertLandable(landableCarried(...))` only after the revert head's own required checks pass (read via `commitChecks` against `branchProtection().requiredChecks` ∪ the culprit's `policy.checks`) — that wait is what makes this lane's bypass the single audited one; hook the runner into `processJob` on `mainGuardIntervalMs` with a deduped `main-guard.failed` event, replacing GY-500's hook once GY-1233 lands. (3) src/daemon/cycle-delivery.ts: under GitHub delivery, when a candidate's failing test gate is explained by a red main (its own run failed on a base a guard window shows red), suppress the GY-831 rework-marking path and record a wait naming the red main instead — the incidents showed every open PR's CI failing churned the queue; and raise exactly one escalation attention line per abandoned revert (action key `main-guard:abandoned:<mergeSha>`, agentOwner('master', 'graphyard master create …'), text naming the merge, the failing check and the revert PR); nothing gates on it. (4) tests/main-guard.test.ts: harness copied from optimistic-merge.test.ts's (fake engine ledger + fake GitHub recording opens/merges/closes, checks per sha): AC-1 — A green then B red asserts B (not A) reverted, B's item reopened with reason naming check+merge sha; AC-2 — conflicting revert (refusal or merge failure) and failing revert checks each close after one attempt, exactly one attention line, and a later red main is handled afresh; plus pending-wait, revert-merge reopen, and bounded-reads assertions. (5) tests/helpers/timing-baseline.json: record only the new file's line (`node scripts/ci-tests.mjs durations`; ci-shards needs ≥90% coverage, the companion test allows exactly this). (6) docs/delivery.md: a tight paragraph under "Pre-merge gate and release-candidate validation" stating how main is kept green under GitHub delivery and what the operator sees when a revert cannot merge — 87 words of headroom, so write ~60–80 words or trim in-page; add a matching REQUIRED_STATEMENTS regex to tests/docs-budget.test.ts; keep every JSON sample parsing (tests/delivery-docs.test.ts). Settled engineering choices: ledger kinds `main-guard.*`; abandon (not retry) on first failed revert; first-culprit-only revert with later merges re-judged on their own commits; guard reads cached per sha and re-read only while pending.

patterns.pattern: Optimistic-merge main guard (GY-500): required suite read on every merge commit of main; window since last green commit; first failing merge reverted via a revert PR the App lands head-bound; item reopened for rework. The direct in-repo ancestor, including its known flaw: a revert that cannot merge holds everything forever (PR #443)

Repair lane (GY-406): the only existing audited bypass lane — App publishes its own check verdict naming why the head may land, then merges head-bound with expectedHeadOid. The new guard's bypass must stay this narrow: bypass verdict only after the revert's own required checks pass, every step on the ledger

git revert of a merge commit uses first parent (-m 1): restore each changed file to its first parent's version — exactly what GitHub.openRevert builds tree-wise; squash merges have one parent and revert as ordinary commits

GitHub REST 'Create a commit revert' endpoint exists as an alternative to hand-building the revert tree; the in-repo tree-building approach is proven with the App token and refuses unclean reverts, so prefer it

GitHub's own fix for this failure class is the merge queue's 'require branches to be up to date' setting; this repository deliberately runs without it under GitHub delivery, so a post-merge guard is the alternative — the same trade bors makes

Chromium's commit queue auto-reverts the culprit of a failed post-merge tree and reopens the CL for rework — same shape: revert the first bad commit, notify with the failing check, never block other work on the revert
Head-bound merge binding (expectedHeadOid) so the App merges exactly the revert commit it built and refuses a moved head — reused unchanged from mergeRevert

Overdue-pending recording (recordRevertPending): a revert waiting on its own CI records one pending event and re-records only when overdue past the observed CI duration — reuse so the waiting guard is visible without spam
Value-identity ledger dedup: Postgres jsonb reorders keys, so event identity is built from values (identity() in guardMain) — required for the new guard's state and attention rows
Daemon one-attention-line idiom: record() with a stable action key carrying culprit identity, `since` for unchanged refusals, and state transitions; re-armed when the key's subject changes

questions.why: It sets the blast radius of automated reverts: reverting all of the window is safer for greenness but throws away innocent merges; reverting only the first culprit keeps the rest, which their own merge commits' runs can re-judge
questions.question: When main breaks under GitHub delivery, does the guard revert only the first failing merge since the last green commit, or every merge in the red window?
questions.recommendation: Revert only the first failing merge (AC-1 says 'exactly that merge'); later merges stay and are judged by their own commits' push runs once the revert lands

questions.why: It decides whether a red main that the guard could not fix waits for an agent decision or a person, and what the AC-3 'what the operator sees' text promises
questions.question: Who owns the stuck-revert attention line — the master agent (files a fix item itself) or the human operator?
questions.recommendation: Master-owned, matching the autonomy contract: agentOwner('master', 'graphyard master create FILE REASON …') with the merge, failing check and revert PR named; a human is never asked to run a command an agent may run

questions.why: Whole-repository limits break on any merge, not only Graphyard deliveries; but only Graphyard items can be 'reopened', so non-Graphyard culprits exercise a different recovery path
questions.question: Should the guard also revert merges made outside Graphyard (a hand-merged or dependabot PR) when they break main?
questions.recommendation: Judge every main merge commit (main's greenness is the goal): open and merge the revert for any culprit, reopen the item when the culprit is a Graphyard delivery, and name it in the audit/attention when it is not

questions.why: It defines 'handles the next red main afresh': the guard must never loop on the same culprit, but it also should not permanently ignore a still-red main the master's fix did not cure
questions.question: When a revert cannot merge and the guard gives up, should the reverted window be retried once main is green again by other means, or does the incident end with the one attention line?
questions.recommendation: End the incident with the attention line; arm again only on a new last-green commit after main passes once — the abandoned window is never retried automatically

questions.why: Faster ticks restore green main sooner (every open PR's CI is red meanwhile) but spend check-run reads every tick; the rate budget is shared with observations

reviews.body:
Follow-up finding: src/server/doctor-route.ts:43 — a retried POST after a committed-but-lost response inserts a duplicate run summary and per-item events; key the insert on run.at.
Follow-up finding: integrations/pi/index.ts:435 — doctorCommandWords takes the first non-option word as the command, so `graphyard --opt status master merge` is judged as the read-only `status` even if the CLI would parse `--opt status` as an option value and run `master merge`; judge the CLI's actual subcommand position (the operator-agent route guard still refuses merge server-side).
Follow-up finding: tests/soak.test.ts:2305 — moving `const items` up truncated the GY-883 comment, which now ends mid-sentence above an unrelated declaration.

Independent Graphyard review of GY-711 at 9382fc6fad3ed2c97929d4ca80c54001966b49a4, against base 48efbe0c63, policy revision 6. I read it in a detached checkout of that commit.

Since the last review (815a2c44), the only GY-711 commit is 9382fc6fad. It changes 4 lines in docs/master-agent.md and docs/onboarding.md. Everything else came from merging main. The doctor code, the remedies, the route and the tests are unchanged, so the earlier code judgements and thread classifications still stand.

## Criteria

- **AC-1: MET.** The new `src/daemon/doctor.ts` adds the doctor role. It is in `registryRoles` and proposed for Pi, and the profile setting `run.doctor` defaults to enabled, 10 min, Pi `model` plus a stronger `fallbackModel`. `doctorStep` runs at cycle step 7d. The operator-agent credential is passed by path. The shipped `doctorPrompt` template names every bound (10/60/20/5/2/30/5/10 min, lapsed containment, stale refusal, overdue). The Pi extension's allowlist permits only `master scope|requirements|unblock|decide|approver|settle-containment|close|create|release` plus reads. Merge, dispatch, evidence and lease commands are refused with a "record it, not run" reason. `unit:doctor-scheduled-and-scoped` covers this.

reviews.body:
Follow-up finding: src/provider-usage.ts:373 — the `allAccounts.length <= 1` branch gives a lone `pi-X` the plan `zai-X` when it is derived alone, as with `observeAccount`'s default `[account]`, but the same account derives a different plan when the registry holds other accounts. The planId an account reports to quota checks then depends on registry size, not on the account.
Follow-up finding: tests/gy-1158-review-followups.test.ts:180 — the finding-3 test checks only `accountSchema`, never the fleet form's request body, so a regression in `web/pages/fleet.tsx` would go undetected.

Independent review of GY-1158 at 641f480236a98c7eef29995d9b1db12656d98352.

## Acceptance criteria

**[AC-1] Each follow-up listed in the description is addressed in code, or declined with a recorded reason: UNMET.**

Here is each follow-up from the GY-1121 review:
- Finding 1 (provider-usage plan sharing by suffix): addressed. `deriveAccountPlan` now needs Z.AI credential evidence on both siblings before it groups them, and `detectPlanKind` checks Claude/Anthropic first.
- Finding 2 (do not treat unrelated auth or process-wide `ZAI_API_KEY` as the account's Z.AI login): **not correctly addressed.** It also brings a regression that undoes the intent of finding 1. See BLOCKING below.
- Finding 3 (fleet form sends null plan): addressed. `web/pages/fleet.tsx` now leaves `plan` out when it is blank.
- Finding 4 (stale exhausted observations per plan): addressed in the eligibility outcome, because the newest probe observation on the plan wins. The side effect is a FOLLOW-UP (thread 2).
- Finding 5 (`observeAccount` passes allAccounts): addressed in `src/fleet.ts`.
- Finding 6 (Pi `{ zai: { key } }` credential, and routing the pi kind to `zaiAccount`): addressed.

## BLOCKING

**PRRT_kwDOUZby-s6opmtq (src/master/environments.ts) blocks AC-1 (findings 1 and 2).** I verified this finding at this head.

With `parallelTips: 4` and no tips in flight, queue positions 2–3 are claimed with the merge path but reported as steady, so master status can understate merge-band lag.

src/github.ts:346 — the 10-minute cadence cap for review requests is a new per-item polling rate, but tests/soak.test.ts asserts no GitHub-read budget for a large review-requested fleet. A soak assertion that the review band stays within its bound without exhausting the pace would guard against regressions.

src/observation-simulation.ts:340 — the simulation computes claim classes once at start, so items never move between bands (a review leading to the merge queue, for example). That is enough for AC-1's steady-state claim but understates churn. A variant that reclassifies items as their readings change would size workers more faithfully.

findings.text: src/stall-remedies.ts:62 — the installation-suspended pattern requires an id between "installation" and "is suspended", so it matches only master-browser.ts's wording; github.ts:919/970 ("App X installation is suspended") and github.ts:887 do not bind and fall back to the generic line.

src/stall-remedies.ts:70 — the worker-credential push shortfall (worker-credential.ts:52, "App X installation lacks …") is not recognised by the permission-hold pattern ("App X lacks"), so a row stalled on it keeps the generic line instead of the installation-accept remedy.
src/daemon/cycle-remedies.ts:67 — a remedy shared by several rows launches against rows[0].work only, so the launch's started entry and report attribute a multi-item flow to the first item alone.

src/model/liveness.ts:417 — after a refused-remedy escalation is answered and the row reopens, a fresh stall on the same reason starts a new run and the remedy is applied again; this is bounded by human answers, but no test pins the cadence.

document.title: Recurring review-convergence faults: 3 in 24 hours

judgement.reason: Real structural work: the recurring pair of review-conflict instances (GY-1092 2026-10-03T03:33Z, GY-1052 04:12Z) each show two APPROVED verdicts from two reviewer sessions (claude-reviewer, opencode-reviewer) posting through the one graphyard-reviewer[bot] identity for the same request — they agree, yet src/model/review-conflict.ts reconcileReviewConflict raises a conflict on any two standing verdicts with the same identity+requestId, withholds BOTH approvals from the gates, and resolves only via a fresh review; it never compares verdict states. The product should settle agreeing verdicts itself (act on the newest) instead of spending a third reviewer round per race. Not fixed by GY-1083: that fix (PR #557, merged 03:08Z, commit b82b58119b) only stops a second reviewer launch after a settlement, and both conflicts occurred after that merge. The third instance (merge-base-dismissed on GY-1136) is already handled by the tree-identical carry/republish path (src/coordination.ts:213, github.ts guard — the tip was republished onto 362a6ef3c1), so the residual work is the agreeing-verdict reconciliation. No open item covers it (GY-1098 is base-sync for workflow files, GY-1008 is blocker re-checking, GY-1072 parallel reviews is delivered and is the amplifier). Priority 2, not 1: today's remedy self-heals via a fresh review, but it stalls already-approved candidates and wastes reviewer capacity, and the class recurred within 25 minutes of the previous class delivery.

findings.text: **<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub> Scope access to the worker's Git credential** When the documented administrator `gh` login is stored in the same unlocked Secret Service keyring, `--talk

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub> Preserve the proxy socket across service restarts** If `xdg-dbus-proxy` crashes or exits when the real session bus restarts while a worker is active, `Re

tests/coordinator-os-confinement.test.ts:192 — the title of `unit:allocated-checkout-re-exposed` lost its space after the em dash ("—a reviewer"). The proof id prefix is unchanged, but the full test title now differs from earlier evidence and from the other titles' style.

deploy/systemd/graphyard-secrets-bus-filter.service:21 — sessions with no credential of their own (master, approver, proof-producer) can still call SearchItems and GetSecret on any unlocked item in the operator's keyring, including the admin `gh` login. A per-session credential broker for those roles would close the remaining read exposure that the original P1 described.

deploy/systemd/graphyard-secrets-bus.socket:6 — an install that already enabled the old `graphyard-secrets-bus.service` must be migrated by hand (disable the service, enable the socket). Nothing in the launcher detects a non-socket-held endpoint, so a host that skips this step keeps the old restart-unlink behaviour unnoticed.

src/master/launch.ts:155 — keyringEndpointWarning runs a `systemctl --user show` with a 10 s timeout on every confined launch that binds the endpoint and repeats the same warning each time; caching the verdict per process (or per endpoint inode) would avoid repeated probes and log noise on an unmigrated host.

src/master/dispatch.ts:181 — `ownGitHubCredential: !!credential` silently gives a worker launched without a minted credential the keyring proxy; whether that fallback should exist at all for workers is worth an explicit decision and test.

src/master/launch.ts:472 — when the probe fails or no user manager answers, null is cached as the socket's final verdict. If the user manager becomes reachable later in the same launcher process, the unmigrated endpoint is never reported. A verdict that "cannot be judged" should not be cached.
